title: Dukkha, Rollercoasters and Nonduality
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart encourages listeners to approach life's challenges with patience, humility, and a non-dualistic mindset, recognizing that our experiences are part of a larger reality that transcends individual perspectives. By acknowledging the complexity and interconnectedness of all things, we can cultivate compassion and understanding for ourselves and others, and work towards ending suffering. This involves embracing both joy and pain as an integral part of life, rather than trying to separate or resist them.

On to past, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept.
I vow to taste the truth of the Tatakara's words.
Good morning and thank you for being here and sharing this absolutely gorgeous, stunning Pacific Northwest morning.
There was a little bit of a struggle because technology kind of threw a wrinkle into the fabric of the universe.
My printer didn't print, and my old laptop—I decided that this was the perfect time to update the HP support website—didn't work either.
So, it became a two-laptop operation.
One second, please.
I recognize that this is kind of awkward, but please have patience.
It's quite appropriate that the title of today's Dharma talk is Dukkha Roller Coasters and Nonduality.
I hope that you and your loved ones are well.
Now, I'm wishing you all the very best.
Together, we are creeping up on the end of the year 2021. 2021 has been quite the roller coaster for many.
We think that some things are getting better, others are getting worse, and so on.

Society, politics, economics, climate justice, racial justice—we have experienced celebration, frustration, getting what is wanted, getting what is disliked, unfulfilled expectations, and undelivered communications.
Forwarded intentions, and key issues that have moved in the right direction, didn't move fast enough or far enough.
In other words, life is serving us a nice thick dukkha stew.
Dukkha, from the Pali, please have patience if you have heard me say this before once or twice or five or ten times.
Dukkha is usually and pretty badly translated as suffering.
Not so, my friends.
Dukkha is much more subtle.
The Buddha said this: "Birth is dukkha.
Aging is dukkha.
Death is dukkha.
Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are dukkha.
Association with the unbeloved is dukkha.
Separation from the loved is dukkha.
Not getting what is wanted is dukkha."
In short, the five clinging aggregates are dukkha.

This list was compiled by a friend's story.
Back to roller coasters.
I used to live in Santa Cruz, and actually so did Tim.
In Santa Cruz, on the boardwalk, is one of the big old classic wooden roller coasters, the Giant Dipper.
I rode it quite a few times, and it was a lot of fun.
Sometimes I would be just outside the boardwalk, and I would watch people enjoy their terror.
After all, they paid good money for the privilege of being scared.
They knew they would be scared.
During the ride, some were so scared that they had to show to everybody that they were not afraid by raising up their arms and waving.
Some would cover their eyes, and some just screamed.
The Giant Dipper is very safe.
After all, many, many thousands have been riding the Giant Dipper since 1924, and it is truly safe unless you squirm out of your seat in the parking lot and you have a lock bar.
It does take serious effort.

So there is a difference whether you are on a roller coaster for the first time, or the tenth time, or whether you are a parent who just does it to make the kids happy, or to complete a day on the beach, or maybe you are just standing outside watching people being scared.
I believe that 2021 is experienced differently by different people, and it is a lot like riding the Giant Dipper.
Some are glad about the outcome of the elections; some were not.
Some were super happy about receiving the vaccines; others were absolutely against them.
Some did not leave the house much, while others went to pool parties packed in like sardines, or they went to the motorcycle valley in Sturges.
Most people gladly wore face masks to protect themselves and their families and their loved ones.
Some violently refused them and compared the situation to wearing the Star of David in Nazi Germany.
I myself have friends whose view of the world and opinions about all this are very different from mine.
They see the world differently.
Sometimes I felt, and I continue to feel, tempted to impose my opinions and views unasked, to be a little bit pushy about vaccinations and masks and so on.
But after so many years of Zen practice, I am certain that this may not be such a good idea.
If I am asked, or when it is appropriate, yes, I will share my perspective.
But more often nowadays, I do not.
Whatever I may say will set up more pros and cons, harden opinions on the other side, causing ruts and trenches to be dug deeper.
And I am aware that whatever I say will not be exactly correct.
How could it be?
Zen master Shunryu Suzuki said this: "Even though you try to put people under control, it is impossible.
You cannot do it.
The best way to control people is to be able to control them.
The best way to control people is to encourage them to be mischievous.
Then they will be in control in a wider sense.
To give your sheep or cow a large spacious meadow is the way to control him."
So it is with people.
First, let them do what they want and watch them.
To ignore them is not good; that is the worst policy.
The second worst is trying to control them.
The best is to watch them, just to watch them without trying to control them.
As Zen Buddhists, we practice every day, year after year.
And the hours we spend on the cushion or the chair sink in deeper and deeper.
Those hours color everything we do and experience.
Zazen will penetrate deeper and deeper and deeper, often not even noticed by us.
It pervades our everyday life.
Zazen teaches us to forget all gaining ideas, all dualistic ideas.
I would like to read you a poem I very much love.
A small book of Inuit poetry was given to me by my good friend Ken Brunton, and this poem or song was in it.
Strangely enough, it was written down and translated around the time the Giant Dipper in Santa Cruz was built.
It is a song from South Baffin Island, attributed to the report of the fifth truly expedition, 1921 to 1924.
And this is the poem.
The kayakers among you will appreciate it.
And I think over again:
*My small adventures went from a shore wind.
I drifted out in my kayak, and I thought I was in danger.
My fears, those small ones that I thought so big, for all the vital things I had to get and to reach.
And yet, there's only one great thing, the only thing, to live and see in huts and on journeys, the great day that dawns, and the light that fills the world.*
Let me read that one more time.
And I think over again:
*My small adventures went from a shore wind.
I drifted out in my kayak, and I thought I was in danger.
My fears, those small ones that I thought so big, for all the vital things I had to get and to reach.
And yet, there's only one great thing, the only thing, to live and see in huts and on journeys, the great day that dawns, and the light that fills the world.*

This Inuit poem is about humility in the face of great forces, in which we humbly acknowledge the smallness of being, which can lead to greater insight into the world, the external, the kayak, and into the sea.
By the shore wind, shore wind comes from the land, and it pushes the kayak out and into the open sea.
And I tell you, when the wind hits a certain speed, there's only one direction you will go, and that is with the wind.
Anything else, you're overpowered.
Happened to me once on the Great Lakes when I was kayaking around on a big island there.
It was a bit scary and hairy.
But the poet counters this external, whereas the internal, which is the journey home to safety.
There is an understanding of the world which is not predicated on domination, not on winning.
The poem is built around dualities: interior and huts, and exterior, the ocean; water and land; danger and salvation; small adventures and the great day; light and dawn; life and potential death.
However, the conclusion is not dualistic.
The other side is favored.
All that is left is constant movement.
All that is left is the dance.
And when we dance, we don't speed up.
The song, so we will done sooner or end up in a special place.
It is just the doing of it.
The poem does not deny danger or external forces, causes and conditions.

I believe whoever created this poem had both feet firmly planted on the ice, and yet there is only one great thing, the only thing, to live and see in huts and on journeys, the great day that dawns, and the light that fills the world.
There is another wonderful nonduality I'm pretty sure most of you know, and it's truly dedicated to nonduality.
Thich Nhat Hanh is a master of it.
Please call me by my true names.
It's an elegant application of skillful means to teach the dharma to the world at large.
The beloved poem teaches impermanence, no self, dependent origination, and deep empathy.
Please call me by my true names.
Don't say that I will depart tomorrow.
Even today I am still arriving.
Look deeply.

Every second I am arriving, to be a bud on a spring branch, to be a tiny bird with still fragile wings learning to sing in my new nest, to be a caterpillar in the heart of a flower, to be a jewel hiding itself in a stone.
I still arrive in order to laugh and to cry, to fear and to hope.
The rhythm of my heart is the birth and death of all that is alive.
I am a mayfly metamorphosing on the surface of the river, and I am the bird that swoops down to swallow the mayfly.
I am a frog swimming happily in the clear water of the pond, and I am the grass snake that silently feeds itself on the frog.
I am the child in Uganda, all skin and bones, my legs as thin as bamboo sticks, and I am the arms merchant selling deadly weapons to Uganda.
I am the twelve-year-old girl, refugee on a small boat, who throws herself into the ocean after being raped by a sea pirate, and I am also the pirate, my heart not yet capable of seeing and loving.
I am a member of the Politburo with plenty of power in my hands, and I am the man who has to pay his debt of blood to my people, dying slowly in a forced labor camp.
My joy is like spring, so warm, it makes flowers bloom all over the earth.
My pain is like a river of tears, so vast it fills the four oceans.
Please, please call me by my true names, so I can hear all my cries and laughter at once, so I can see that my joy and pain are one.
Please call me by my true names, so I can wake up in the door to my heart, I left open the door of compassion.
I hope you found something in this talk that may be useful to you.
And if you didn't, please forget every single word.
And thank you for listening.
May our intention equally extend to every being and place.
This is the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's ways unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.
